content: 1. Expel any air and excess drops from the syringe before proceeding. Tuberculin must be injected within 20 minutes of being drawn into the syringe. 2. To administer the tuberculin injection, first clean the selected site gently with an alcohol swab. Stretch the skin at the site using the thumb and forefinger. Insert the needle slowly with the bevel facing upwards at an angle of 5–15 degrees. Advance the needle approximately 3 mm into the epidermis until the entire bevel is covered and visible just beneath the skin. Release the stretched skin and inject the tuberculin slowly, checking for any leakage. Once 1 mL of solution has been administered, remove the needle quickly. 3. If a drop of blood appears at the injection site, gently blot it with an alcohol-based disinfectant without squeezing out the tuberculin. 4. After the injection, check the site. A correctly administered injection will produce a pale wheal measuring 6–10 mm in diameter. If the wheal is less than 6 mm, the test should be repeated at a site at least 5 cm away from the original site. 5. The tuberculin skin test (TST) should be read 48–72 hours after injection, but not before 48 hours or after 72 hours. The forearm should be slightly flexed at the elbow during the reading, and the test should be performed in good lighting conditions. 6. To assess the presence of induration (a palpable, raised, hardened area or swelling), begin with visual inspection and then palpate the area gently. Use the fingertips to locate the edges of the induration by sweeping in all four directions. Mark the widest edges of the induration lightly with a fine line or dot. If the margins are irregular, measure the widest diameter. 7. Measure the diameter of the induration across the forearm, from the thumb side to the little finger side, using a plastic ruler. Place the zero line of the ruler inside the edge of the marked line or dot and measure to the opposite edge. If the measurement falls between two divisions on the millimeter scale, record the lower division. Do not measure redness, swelling, or bruising—only the induration. 8. Alternatively, the ballpoint pen method can be used to determine the outer limit of the induration. Draw a line with a ballpoint pen on the transverse axis of the forearm, starting 1–2 cm away from the visible reaction and moving slowly toward its center while applying moderate pressure. The point where resistance to pen movement occurs marks the outer edge of the induration. Mark the widest edges and measure the diameter as described above. 9. Record the location of the TST administration (right or left forearm). If no induration is present, record the result as zero. Otherwise, record the exact size of the induration in millimeters. Do not record the result as positive or negative. Note any adverse events at the test site, such as vesicles, bullae, lymphangitis, ulceration, or necrosis. 10. The TST does not measure immunity to tuberculosis (TB) but rather the degree of hypersensitivity to tuberculin. The interpretation of the test result depends on the individual’s risk of TB infection and progression to disease, as well as the size of the induration in millimeters. There is no correlation between the size of the induration and the likelihood of current TB disease or future risk of developing TB. Similarly, there is no correlation between the size of TST reactions post-BCG vaccination and protection against TB. 11. Induration of ≥5 mm is considered positive in children living with HIV or those who are severely malnourished (e.g., with clinical evidence of marasmus or kwashiorkor). Induration of ≥10 mm is considered positive in all other children, regardless of BCG vaccination status. 12. A negative TST result may indicate the absence of infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis or that the infection is recent and the body has not yet developed a reaction to the test. The window period from infection to the development of cell-mediated immunity can be up to 12 weeks, during which the TST may be negative. Immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV and low CD4 T-cell counts or severe malnutrition, often show negative TST results due to anergy or lack of previous sensitization. 13. Vesicles, bullae, lymphangitis, ulceration, or necrosis at the test site may indicate a high degree of tuberculin sensitivity and the presence of TB infection.
